title: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
gist: AWS's EC2 kernel team triages a flood of Linux kernel CVEs (about 16 a day since the kernel became a CNA) in stages. A non-AI script drops about 70% of them, an AI agent classifies the rest in about 3.4 seconds each with an estimated 5-10% problematic decisions, and humans review the output. AWS's data shows older LTS branches carry far more unfixed CVEs (1,709 on 5.10 vs 229 on 6.18), which is pushing it to upgrade kernels faster.

insights.claim: After the Linux kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority in February 2024, kernel CVEs went from about two a week to about 16 a day, with 848 published on 15 August 2026 alone.
insights.so_what: Kernel CVE volume has grown roughly 50-fold, overwhelming manual triage and creating demand for automated vulnerability management.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders

insights.claim: The kernel CVE documentation says the project cannot know how a given system uses the kernel, so users must decide for themselves which CVEs apply to them.
insights.so_what: The cost of triage falls on every operator, which favours managed platforms and vendors who can absorb it.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders

insights.claim: AWS's first triage stage uses no AI: a script reads the kernel's JSON CVE records and discards any CVE outside the affected version range or touching files not built into the image, removing about 70% of CVEs.
insights.speaker: Justinien Bouron
insights.so_what: Simple deterministic filtering does most of the work, so AI is the second stage, not the core.

insights.claim: The AWS agent is given the kernel source tree, per-platform configs, a threat model and a severity rubric, and fills in a table of affected subsystem, vulnerability type and attack vector. The team ignores CVSS scores because they are not specific to its environment.
insights.speaker: Justinien Bouron
insights.so_what: Generic CVSS-based tooling loses ground to triage tailored to each environment.
insights.quote: "We're really using it as a very fancy classifier."

insights.claim: The AWS agent takes about 3.4 seconds per CVE against minutes for a person, so human review by two engineers is now the slowest step, and the team does not plan to remove it.
insights.speaker: Justinien Bouron
insights.so_what: Human verification stays the bottleneck, which limits how much security headcount AI can replace.
insights.quote: "We don't want to hinge our entire security posture on the output of an LLM agent."

insights.claim: Bouron informally estimated that 5% to 10% of the AWS agent's triage decisions were problematic; no formal evaluation was presented.
insights.speaker: Justinien Bouron
insights.so_what: Error rates are still material, so human review stays and fully autonomous security operations claims deserve scepticism.

insights.claim: Microsoft's Azure Linux team takes triage verdicts from a rule table, with AI only suggesting its inputs. Its backporting agents went from about 50% to 80% success after adding a build-and-test feedback loop.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Agent success depends heavily on verification loops, which is where tooling value lies.

insights.claim: Google DeepMind's CodeMender focuses on writing fixes, and human researchers review every patch before it is submitted upstream.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Big players all keep a human in the loop, a sign of how mature AI security automation really is.

insights.claim: Disabling unneeded kernel features to cut the number of applicable CVEs is deceptively difficult: there are more than 32,000 configuration options, and removing the wrong one can cause bugs or performance regressions that appear months later.
insights.speaker: Justinien Bouron
insights.so_what: Hardening by minimisation is costly, which favours large operators with tight control over their workloads.

insights.claim: Backporting fixes in-house is risky because CVE records often name only the final fixing commit, so a team that misses prerequisite commits can stay vulnerable after applying the listed fix.
insights.speaker: Justinien Bouron
insights.so_what: Staying on old kernels carries hidden security risk and argues for upgrading faster.

insights.claim: For CVEs affecting all six branches studied, the median time from a mainline fix to an LTS release was 31.8 days for Linux 5.10 versus 18.1 days for 6.18. On 16 September, 5.10 had 1,709 known unfixed CVEs against 229 for 6.18.
insights.so_what: Running older LTS kernels builds up security debt, an argument for faster upgrades across enterprise fleets.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders

insights.claim: AWS's kernel upgrades keep getting faster: 4.19 to 5.10 took about two years, the next upgrade about a year, and the move to 6.18 about six months. The team now plans to move the fleet as each new LTS release appears.
insights.speaker: Dylan Johnson
insights.so_what: Faster upgrade cadence is becoming a practical security requirement at hyperscalers.

insights.claim: During AWS's 5.10-to-6.12 kernel upgrade, 43% of tracked issues were fixed in userspace, where workloads depended on older kernel behaviour.
insights.speaker: Dylan Johnson
insights.so_what: Much of the cost of an upgrade sits in application compatibility, not the kernel itself.

insights.claim: Host patching and Linux CVE handling are among the hidden burdens of building your own cloud, so organisations should focus on what makes their business valuable to customers.
insights.speaker: Berend de Boer
insights.so_what: The growing patch burden strengthens the economic case for managed cloud over self-hosting.
insights.quote: "Focus on what makes your business valuable to your customers,"
